reason: import paths: the Go TM grammar scopes the quoted path as a string (green). Semantic namespace yellow is the correct meaning and matches ODP's namespace color.

package references (fmt.Println): the Go TM grammar has no package scope, so the qualifier falls through to variable red. Semantic namespace yellow is the correct meaning and matches ODP's namespace color.
consts are orange by design (constants merged into the literal family, ecosystem-majority ruling 2026-07-20); the Go TM grammar cannot see constness
const locals are orange by design (constants merged into the literal family, 2026-07-20); TM only marks some declaration sites
enum members are compile-time constants - orange like variable.readonly (constant/literal merge 2026-07-20); TM has no enum-member awareness and paints them variable red.
constructor calls and defaultLibrary types: TM guesses function-call blue; semantic class yellow keeps the type family consistent (approved look since Record<> screenshot)
ODP paints object receivers (variable.other.object) yellow; semantic cannot opt out per-language, and uniform red has been the shipped look since v0.0.2
same as variable: parameters used as object receivers get TM receiver-yellow
mid-chain properties (a.b.c) get ODP receiver-yellow via variable.other.object.property; same decision as variable receivers: identity-consistent red wins

parameter italic is a deliberate One Dark Pro signature kept on taste (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §6 'Variables, keys, and parameters' / §7); the Go TM grammar has no variable.parameter scope at all, so every parameter goes non-italic -> italic when gopls lands. Colour is unchanged (red both sides).

same ruling as go/parameter: parameter italic is a kept ODP signature (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §6/§7). The TS/JS grammars scope variable.parameter only at some declaration sites (not arrow-function or destructured params, never usages), so the italic arrives with the semantic layer. Colour is unchanged.

same ruling as go/parameter and ts/parameter: parameter italic is a kept ODP signature (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §6/§7). Neither the Rust nor the C++ TM grammar has a variable.parameter scope, so every parameter is non-italic until rust-analyzer/clangd lands. Colour is unchanged.

enum members are compile-time constants - orange like variable.readonly (constant/literal merge 2026-07-20, docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §6). TM paints `Shape::Point` / `Some` type-yellow because it only sees a capitalised path segment; it cannot know the segment is a value.

same constant/literal ruling for tuple-style variants: `Shape::Rect(w, h)` looks like a call to the TM grammar, so the variant gets function-blue. Semantic orange is the honest identity (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §5/§6).
same constant/literal ruling where TM has no enum awareness at all and falls through to variable red (C++ `Kind::Circle`).
trait bounds written like calls (`F: FnMut(&T) -> String`) get function-blue from the Rust TM grammar. A trait is a type, and the type family is yellow (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §6 'Types').

`macro_rules` in `macro_rules! square`: the Rust TM grammar scopes it as the macro's *name* (entity.name.function.macro, blue), but it is the keyword introducing the definition - `square` is the name. Semantic purple corrects a TM misclassification (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §4).

items generated by a macro invocation (`named_pair!(origin_pair, 0, 1)`): to TM the argument is a bare identifier and falls through to variable red; rust-analyzer expands the macro and knows a function is being declared. Exactly the 'semantic fixes what TM could not see' case (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §4).
a closure parameter that is called (`f(it)`) reads as a function call to TM and gets blue. Identity outranks position (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §5): it is a parameter, so it is red.

inline format captures (`println!("{GREETING}")`): TM marks the region meta.interpolation but the theme leaves its interior at string green, so the captured identifier arrives green. Interpolated code is code, not string content (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §6 'Embedded boundaries and strings'), and the theme already accepts semantic paint inside strings via the `string.format` entry (Go's %d placeholders).
same interpolation ruling for the numeric part of a format spec (`{v:>4}`): TM leaves it at string green, semantic makes it a literal (orange).

typed numeric literals (`1.0_f64`): the Rust TM grammar paints the suffix as a type (yellow) while rust-analyzer's `number` token covers the whole literal. A literal's suffix is part of the literal, so the constant/literal orange wins (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §6).
`constexpr`/`const` values are orange by design (constants merged into the literal family, 2026-07-20); the C++ TM grammar cannot see constness and paints them variable red.
ODP paints dot-receivers (variable.other.object) yellow; identity outranks position, so a variable stays red wherever it is written (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §5). Same ruling as the TS entry.
same receiver-yellow ruling as cpp/variable: a parameter used before a dot gets TM receiver-yellow (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §5).
member fields used as receivers (`items_.push_back(...)`) get ODP receiver-yellow; same identity ruling as the TS property entry (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §5).
a member field that TM reads as part of a call expression gets function-blue; it is a field, so it is red (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §5).

class/type names the C++ TM grammar cannot recognise (`Vec2 a{...}`, `std::string`) fall through to variable red. The type family is yellow (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §6 'Types'); this is semantic fixing a TM misclassification.
constructors and constructor calls read as function calls to TM (blue). Same ruling as the TS class entry: the type family stays yellow.
`enum class Kind` used as a qualifier: TM has no enum-type scope and falls through to variable red; an enum is a type, so it is yellow (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §6).

builtin and library type names spelled like storage keywords (`auto`, `size_t`, `uint8_t`) are storage.type in the C++ grammar and therefore keyword-purple. Ruling on record: 'a type is yellow because it is a type, not because of how it is spelled' - explicitly including builtin primitives (docs/PHILOSOPHY.md §6 'Types', which cites Go's int/string/error for the same reason).

macro *usages* have no scope of their own in the C++ grammar and fall through to variable red; the theme's `macro` entry (blue) is the deliberate colour for the family, and only clangd can tell a macro from a variable.
